title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22098v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.
relevance_reason: Key author: Rafael G\'omez-Bombarelli

title: An open dataset of gas adsorption in deformable metal-organic frameworks for direct air capture
abstract:
arXiv:2508.03162v3 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Engineering economical and scalable processes for direct air capture (DAC) from humid air relies on atomistic modeling to search and identify promising sorbent materials from a vast chemical space. Machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for predicting material properties in an efficient yet accurate manner, but these models require large sets of carefully curated training data. We present the Open DAC 2025 (ODAC25) dataset comprising nearly 60 million DFT single-point calculations for CO2, H2O, N2, and O2 adsorption in ~15,000 MOFs. ODAC25 introduces functionalized MOFs, high-energy adsorbate placements, and synthetically generated frameworks to maximize the versatility of models trained on the dataset. ODAC25 improves upon the accuracy of DFT calculations in previous works and applies engineering intuition from recent work regarding the treatment of adsorbate-induced MOF flexibility. We release state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials trained on ODAC25 and demonstrate their utility via Henry's coefficient predictions. ODAC25 enables MOF screening for DAC at a resolution previously unattainable.

title: Prior-guided adaptive local refinement of foundation interatomic potentials
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22626v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Foundation interatomic potentials enable simulations across diverse materials, but task-specific inaccuracies can require additional first-principles data. Obtaining these data is challenging when the relevant local environments arise in large simulation cells. Here we introduce the Prior-guided Adaptive Refinement Scheme (PARS), which identifies weakly supported environments during molecular dynamics by comparing their frozen representations with prototypes of pretraining environments, without requiring initial task labels or model ensembles. Selected environments are reconstructed as compact periodic cells for first-principles labelling and iterative refinement. Applications to phase stability, surface migration and vacancy clustering show improvements in target properties, including an 81% reduction in the mean absolute error of Ti vacancy-cluster energies per vacancy relative to the pretrained model. For Si/Ge, a foundation potential refined using 800 labelled cells containing 10-128 atoms is subsequently distilled into a compact potential without additional first-principles training labels. In simulations containing approximately 362,880 atoms, the distilled model predicts an interfacial thermal resistance consistent with that of a potential trained directly on density-functional theory data. These results demonstrate a route for adapting foundation potentials to target applications through local reference calculations.
relevance_reason: Develops and applies an adaptive refinement/distillation workflow for foundation ML interatomic potentials using MD and DFT labeling on explicit atomistic cells, satisfying (a)-(c).

title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22272v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.
relevance_reason: Popcornn optimizes continuous neural-network reaction paths on machine-learned interatomic potentials to locate transition states, benchmarked against NEB and growing string on thousands of organic reactions; (a) explicit atoms yes, (b) MLIP-driven TS/NEB search plus method development yes, (c) advances transition-state search methodology yes.

title: Dynamics and transport in LiF using classical and machine learned interatomic potentials
abstract:
arXiv:2611.21900v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We perform molecular dynamics simulations of molten Lithium Fluoride, comparing the classical Buckingham and Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials with machine-learnt interatomic potentials - the MACE-MP-0b3 (small) foundation model potential, and a fine-tuned version thereof. We find that the MACE-MP-0b3, out-of-the-box, is able to accurately reproduce the experimental shear viscosity across the liquid state comparable with polarisable potentials despite not itself being polarisable. Previous viscosities computed using classical potentials are under-predicted, which has previously been attributed to a suppressed melting temperature. Prompted by this we compare the melting points of these potentials. We find that the machine-learnt potentials address the significant underestimation of the melting point of the classical potentials, though the refined potential and the foundation model differ significantly between themselves. We probe the microscopic structure and dynamics of each model to further elucidate the considerable change in viscosity between classical and machine-learnt potentials. We find that, despite their lower melting temperature, classical potentials produce considerably stiffer, higher frequency, single-particle and collective charge-transport dynamics on account of their fixed charges. However, in the long-wavelength limit, the many-body machine-learnt potentials feature more elastic collective motion that governs the diffusion of momentum and is therefore responsible for the enhanced shear viscosity.
relevance_reason: Classical MD of molten LiF comparing Buckingham/Born-Huggins-Mayer potentials against MACE-MP-0b3 MLIPs, including melting points, viscosity, and transport; (a) explicit atoms, (b) MD plus MLIP benchmarking/application, and (c) both a force-field comparison and a physical study of the system, all satisfied.

title: Combined magnetic and structural transition state in first-principles calculations
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22489v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present a generalized nudged elastic band (NEB) implementation within potential-based constrained density-functional theory (cDFT) for calculating transition pathways that simultaneously optimize atomic, lattice, and magnetic degrees of freedom. Unlike standard fixed-cell NEB calculations restricted to atomic displacements, our framework consistently couples atomic forces, stresses, and spin torques. The method supports fixed- and variable-cell approaches for collinear and non- collinear magnetic configurations, by incorporating magnetic torques and generalized cell coordinates within the NEB optimization. To validate the methodology, we present benchmark calculations for representative magnetostructural systems. Specifically, we investigate the bcc-to-hcp transformation in Fe and the antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic transition in FeRh using the variable-cell formalism. Furthermore, we examine spin-reversal processes in two-dimensional CrI3 to analyze the influence of spin-orbit coupling on transition paths and their associated energy barriers.
relevance_reason: Develops a generalized NEB implementation in constrained DFT coupling atomic, cell, and magnetic degrees of freedom, benchmarked on Fe, FeRh, and CrI3; explicit atoms (a), NEB/DFT method development (b), and method advance plus applications (c) all satisfied.

title: Stein Kernelized Molecular Dynamics for Active Learning of Interatomic Potentials
abstract:
arXiv:2606.04100v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) enable efficient and accurate atomistic simulations but depend critically on the quality and diversity of the training data. We introduce Stein kernelized molecular dynamics (SKMD), an enhanced sampling method that uses interacting particle dynamics to acquire informative training configurations for the fine-tuning of MLIPs. SKMD corresponds to a stochastic variant of Stein variational gradient descent that is adapted for molecular dynamics by incorporating asynchronous particle updates and a kernel of global atomic descriptors, which provides a symmetry-aware measure of configurational similarity. Unlike other enhanced samplers used in molecular dynamics, SKMD maintains the Boltzmann distribution as a stationary distribution of its dynamics in the appropriate asymptotic limit. This property enforces a balance between the exploration of diverse configurations and attraction toward high-probability regions of the energy landscape. We further propose an approach to efficient online data acquisition using an adaptive stopping criterion that selects non-redundant training data over the course of simulation. We demonstrate SKMD for the active learning of a neural network model of the M\"uller--Brown potential, a MACE interatomic potential for alanine dipeptide, and a MACE foundation model with a DFT oracle for predicting the Pandey reconstruction of the Si(111) surface. Compared to active learning baselines, our method achieves higher model accuracy in fewer training iterations.
relevance_reason: Stein-kernelized MD is an enhanced-sampling/active-learning method for acquiring training configurations for MLIPs (MACE, foundation models, DFT oracle), directly satisfying (a) explicit atoms, (b) MLIP training and MD sampling, and (c) method advance.

title: Ab initio  reaction pathways and nonadiabatic cycloreversion dynamics in 2-styrylthiophene
abstract: We report a combined electronic-structure and nonadiabatic molecular dynamics investigation of the excited-state nonradiative decay processes in 2-styrylthiophene (2-STTP). The ground and excited state conformational landscapes were characterized at second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation and the algebraic diagrammatic construction to second-order [ADC(2)] levels with the aug-cc-pVDZ basis set. To identify the key relaxation channels governing ultrafast deactivation, minimum-energy conical intersections between the S1 and S0 states were optimized at the complete active space self-consistent field level. Twisted-pyramidalized and cyclized-like MECIs relevant to photoisomerization and photocyclization are located and analyzed. The connectivity between conformers and MECIs was further explored using geodesic interpolation reaction paths, which reveal that isomerization channels originating from cis conformers are more favorable than those from trans conformers, and the cyclized MECIs can be accessed with comparatively small or even barrierless energy profiles. To complement these static insights, trajectory-based ab initio molecular dynamics simulations were carried out to study the cycloreversion reaction for CYC1. The dynamical results demonstrate rapid internal conversion within 100 fs and highlight a strong competition between reactive and nonreactive decay pathways, leading either to open-ring photoproduct formation or recovery of the initial reactant structure. Overall, the combined approach provides a comprehensive mechanistic picture of the excited-state behavior, emphasizing the decisive role of conical intersection accessibility and excited-state potential energy surface topology in controlling photophysical and photochemical outcomes.
relevance_reason: Uses MP2/ADC(2)/CASSCF electronic structure plus trajectory-based ab initio molecular dynamics on explicit 2-styrylthiophene atoms, satisfying (a) explicit atoms, (b) ab initio MD/electronic-structure methods, and (c) mechanistic application.

title: Calculation of interfacial tensions between solid, liquid, and vapor phases in metals by molecular simulations
abstract: The interfacial free energy is a key determinant of material behavior, governing phenomena such as wetting, adhesion, nucleation, and phase coexistence. Despite its importance, experimental measurements remain challenging, particularly for liquid metals and solid–liquid interfaces under extreme conditions. Classical molecular dynamics (CMD) provides a versatile alternative, enabling atomistic evaluation of interfacial properties beyond experimental reach. In this work, we systematically compute solid–vapor, solid–liquid, and liquid–vapor interfacial free energies across multiple metals, applying and comparing established atomistic methods, including both the mechanical and thermodynamic routes, free energy perturbation, and thermodynamic integration. This unified framework allows cross-validation between methods and interfaces, revealing consistent trends and highlighting the influence of interatomic potentials on accuracy. Our results demonstrate the robustness of CMD for interfacial predictions and emphasize the importance of careful potential validation. These findings provide a coherent picture of metallic interfacial thermodynamics, with implications for mesoscale modeling, materials design, and high-temperature applications.
relevance_reason: Classical MD with free-energy perturbation and thermodynamic integration on explicit metal atoms satisfies (a), (b), and (c) by computing interfacial free energies.

title: Implementation of Girsanov Reweighting in CP2K
abstract:
arXiv:2601.05419v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Dynamical reweighting of path measures is a powerful approach for accurately evaluating slow molecular processes using modified potential energy surfaces used in enhanced sampling methods. Integrating this reweighting framework into the CP2K electronic-structure and molecular-dynamics (MD) software package delivers a robust and widely applicable tool for metadynamics, uncertainty quantification, and force-field optimisation based on both \textit{ab initio} and classical MD simulations. Based on the Girsanov theorem for stochastic dynamical systems, the method is adapted to the Bussi-Donadio-Parrinello velocity-rescaling scheme. This scheme is accessible through the CSVR thermostat and can be interpreted as a Langevin OVRVO/OBABO update scheme requiring two random numbers per integration step. Comprehensive implementation details are provided, including a complete overview of the modified CP2K modules involved in the MD cycle and the computation of reweighting factors. The framework supports multiple sources of bias potentials, enabling reweighting via the PLUMED interface or CP2K-native external potentials and restraints. The feasibility of the implementation is demonstrated through rerun benchmarks, dynamical reweighting of Markov state models (MSMs) and computation of transport properties based on CP2K trajectories, showing excellent agreement with reference simulations.
relevance_reason: Implementation of Girsanov dynamical reweighting in CP2K for metadynamics and Markov-state-model analysis of ab initio and classical MD trajectories; (a) explicit atoms, (b) MD plus enhanced-sampling/free-energy methodology, and (c) a clear methodological advance, all satisfied.

title: Supercell periodicity biases octahedral tilting and energetics in high-entropy perovskite oxides
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22313v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Odd-period supercells such as $3 \times 3 \times 5$ are often used for equimolar five-component compositions in computational studies of high-entropy perovskite oxides (HEPOs). However, such cells are known to constrain octahedral tilting because they cannot accommodate all standard tilt patterns (Glazer tilt systems). How strongly this constraint affects HEPOs, whose octahedra respond to local cation environments, remains unclear. Here we show that supercell periodicity systematically biases computed octahedral tilting and energetics. Using a machine-learning interatomic potential, we compared odd-period and tilt-commensurate cells for 13 HEPOs. Odd-period cells yielded smaller and less coherent tilts and higher energies, even after configurational averaging. In ~1,700-atom cells, tilt differences persisted in all compositions and energy differences in most. The bias extended to defects, with lower oxygen vacancy formation energies in odd-period cells for strongly tilted compositions. Based on these findings, a simple design rule for equimolar supercells is proposed to lift this constraint.
relevance_reason: Uses a machine-learned interatomic potential to compute octahedral tilting, energies, and defect formation energies in ~1700-atom high-entropy perovskite supercells; explicit atoms (a), MLIP-driven energetics (b), and a methodological finding about supercell bias (c) are satisfied.

title: AlCoCuFeNi High-Entropy Alloy Nanoparticle Melting and Solidification: A Classical Molecular Dynamics Simulation Study
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22858v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The processes of melting and solidification of an AlCoCuFeNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle with a diameter of about 10 nm were studied by classical molecular dynamics simulation using an embedded atom model potential. Three cooling rates, 10^11, 10^12, and 10^13 K/s, were considered. Melting and crystallization behavior were characterized through the temperature dependence of the potential energy. Structural evolution was analyzed using adaptive common-neighbor analysis (CNA) and radial distribution functions (RDF). The results show that the final structure changes from amorphous to crystalline as the cooling rate decreases. A pronounced temperature hysteresis associated with melting and crystallization was also observed.
relevance_reason: Performs classical molecular dynamics of an AlCoCuFeNi nanoparticle using an EAM potential and analyzes melting/solidification with CNA and RDF, clearly satisfying (a)-(c).

title: When Do Tensor Product Paths Matter? A Group-Theoretic Analysis of Equivariant Interatomic Potentials
abstract:
arXiv:2611.21683v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tensor-product (TP) layers in equivariant interatomic potentials encode angular interactions through symmetry-allowed paths. Yet local site symmetry can make an allowed path carry no signal after neighbor aggregation. We call this effect Aggregation Cancellation. In a scalar-input first layer, equal-species neighbors on a complete site-symmetry orbit share scalar and radial factors, reducing their angular contribution to a spherical-harmonic orbit sum. If the restricted degree-$l$ representation has no trivial component, this sum and the corresponding path vanish for any learned radial weight. For an ideal $O_h$ octahedral orbit, this removes the $l_\mathrm{edge}=1,2,3$ classes. Beyond the first layer, the factorisation no longer holds, so cancellation is no longer guaranteed; we instead ask whether affected paths remain less important on average. We test the two levels separately in NequIP: matched-radius TiO$_6$ probes examine first-layer cancellation, whereas a within-model CaTiO$_3$ comparison and six OMat24 models examine the importance bias. We then rank paths on training frames, choose the pruning fraction on validation frames, and evaluate frozen masks on held-out tests. At the highest evaluated fraction (60% of 174 paths), force mean absolute error (MAE) changes are 1.42%, 0.04%, and 1.83% for CaTiO$_3$, OMat24 $O_h$-cubic, and OMat24 low-symmetry data, respectively. The masks imply 67.12-71.94% potential TP-operation reduction and 59.77% potential edge multilayer perceptron (MLP) reduction; these are structural proxies, not measured speedups. The results connect local symmetry to path redundancy and pruning robustness in NequIP; transfer to other architectures remains open.
relevance_reason: Group-theoretic analysis and path pruning of tensor-product layers in NequIP equivariant interatomic potentials, benchmarked on TiO6 probes, CaTiO3 and OMat24 force MAEs; (a) explicit atoms yes, (b) MLIP development/analysis yes, (c) advances MLIP architecture understanding yes.

title: Efficient strategies for obtaining accurate kinetics from biased simulations
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22137v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: It has been demonstrated that one can recover the unbiased rate constants for slow conformational transitions by observing transitions driven by a bias potential added along one or several collective variables (CVs). However, the choice of CV, biasing scheme, biasing parameters and the rate estimator can all affect the results and it is not obvious which to choose for a given problem. In this study, we compare accuracy versus computational cost for a previously established benchmark system, a coarse-grained protein with computationally accessible unfolding kinetics. We apply bias to four CVs of decreasing quality in both a time-dependent and quasi-static manner, and compare different estimators for the unfolding rate constant in terms of absolute accuracy to the estimated reference unbiased rate. We show that in the case of gentle biasing, the exponential average time-dependent rate (EATR) framework, which simultaneously fits the unbiased rate constant and a coordinate quality metric $\gamma$, recovers accurate kinetics in nearly all cases.For poor CVs, estimators equivalent to assuming a good coordinate ($\gamma=1$) systematically fail regardless of biasing method or parameters. We introduce heuristics to show when we expect the rates to be inaccurate, and identify which combinations of biasing scheme, estimator and number of runs reach a given accuracy at the lowest cost.
relevance_reason: Comparison of biasing schemes, collective variables and rate estimators to recover unbiased unfolding kinetics of a coarse-grained protein from biased molecular dynamics; (a) coarse-grained beads with atomistic mapping yes, (b) enhanced-sampling MD yes, (c) advances free-energy/kinetics methodology yes.

title: Mapping phase competition in GaAs under pressure and temperature
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22332v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pressure-induced transformations in GaAs offer a means to investigate the interplay between crystal structure, electronic behaviour, and phase stability in a technologically important III-V semiconductor. Here, we have used structure search algorithm combined with first-principles calculations and identified high-pressure competitive phases. The previously proposed $Imm2$ structure lies above the calculated minimum-enthalpy envelope. The static enthalpy calculations with the PBEsol functional predict the transition sequence $F\bar{4}3m \rightarrow Cmcm \rightarrow I\bar{4}m2 \rightarrow C2/m \rightarrow Amm2$, at approximately 12, 14, 34, and 69 GPa, respectively. The initial zinc blende to $Cmcm$ transition is accompanied by a volume reduction of approximately 17.5 % and metallization within the PBEsol description. Phonon calculations support the dynamical stability of all five phases at representative pressures, while elastic calculations characterize their mechanical response. Vibrational free energies are incorporated within the quasiharmonic approximation to examine phase competition over 0-80 GPa and 0-1000 K. These results identify competing high-pressure structures and connect their relative energetics with the electronic, vibrational, and elastic responses of compressed GaAs.
relevance_reason: Structure search plus first-principles DFT enthalpy, phonon, elastic, and quasiharmonic free-energy calculations for GaAs polymorphs; explicit atoms (a), DFT-based crystal structure prediction (b), and phase-competition results (c) satisfied.

title: Efficient Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22444v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) reach an accuracy close to quantum mechanical reference calculations at a small fraction of the cost. Efficiency is the purpose of MLIPs, yet strategies for efficient MLIPs have not been reviewed systematically. This review takes efficiency as its guideline. To compare MLIPs on a common footing, we represent them in a complete basis expansion, the Atomic Cluster Expansion (ACE) and its graph generalization (GRACE). The expansion is canonical, built from products of single-particle functions. Classical interatomic potentials, such as the embedded-atom method, and many modern MLIPs, including equivariant transformers, can be represented within this expansion. Much of the apparent diversity of MLIP architectures therefore reflects how non-linearity, layer coupling and optimization are handled rather than which interactions the models can represent. We show how the cost of an MLIP becomes linear in system size and, at fixed rank of the tensor decomposition, in model complexity, and we discuss the role of machine learning, which provides non-linear parameterizations and optimization. Because efficiency is meaningful only at a given accuracy, we also compare accuracy and cost. On the Matbench Discovery leaderboard, models with three to five layers approach the accuracy of deeper models, and one basis, truncated along the Pareto front of error and speed, spans more than two orders of magnitude in cost. Ultimately, training data determine the quality of any MLIP.
relevance_reason: Review systematically comparing MLIP architectures via ACE/GRACE basis and accuracy-cost benchmarks on Matbench Discovery; focused on MLIP development/benchmarking with explicit atomistic many-body expansions, satisfying (a)-(c).

title: A multiscale description of electrical double layers in alkaline hydrogen evolution: From continuum theory to molecular dynamics
abstract: A molecular-level understanding of electrical double-layer (EDL) structure is essential for establishing a physically realistic description of electrochemical interfaces. In this work, we develop an experiment-informed continuum-atomistic framework that integrates experimentally derived hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) kinetics, Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) transport modeling, and atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate interfacial structure evolution under alkaline HER conditions. Unlike many continuum EDL models in which electrostatic boundary conditions are specified independently of interfacial reaction kinetics, the present framework incorporates experimentally extracted HER kinetic parameters through reaction-derived ion-flux boundary conditions, establishing a direct connection between electrochemical kinetics and interfacial ion transport, electrostatic potential, and electric-field distributions. Quantitative comparisons among classical PNP, sterically modified PNP, and MD simulations reveal the progressive influence of finite ion size and molecular-scale hydration on interfacial ion redistribution. While modified PNP recovers physically bounded ion concentrations and improves continuum predictions, they remain unable to capture the nonmonotonic ion distributions and molecular-scale solvent organization resolved by MD simulations. Atomistic simulations further reveal hydration-dependent ion positioning and pronounced water layering near the electrode surface, defining a reaction-relevant interfacial region where molecular effects become dominant. These results quantify the applicability and limitations of continuum descriptions under alkaline HER conditions and provide a framework for connecting electrochemical kinetics with molecular-scale interfacial structures across different length scales.
relevance_reason: Integrates continuum PNP with atomistic MD of explicit interfacial ions/water, satisfying (a) explicit atoms, (b) classical MD, and (c) application to EDL structure in alkaline HER.

title: Swift Heavy Ion Tracks in Polymorphs of Titanium Dioxide: The Effects of Electron Beam and Crystal Structures
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22153v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Swift heavy ion (SHI) irradiation generates nanoscale damage in materials, offering opportunities for controlled modification of structural properties. Understanding the fundamental processes governing damage formation in altered regions remains a longstanding challenge. This work explores how crystal structure influences swift heavy ion-induced damage formation and evolution in rutile and anatase TiO2. Combining transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate how differences in atomic arrangement govern track morphology and structural recovery. Although irradiation produces amorphous tracks in both polymorphs, their morphologies differ considerably. In rutile, tracks develop pronounced diameter variations, forming hourglass-like structures, whereas in anatase they retain a relatively uniform cylindrical shape. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that these differences arise from the distinct recrystallization behavior of the two crystal structures during rapid cooling, leading to different pathways of track evolution and recovery. Particular attention is paid to electron beam induced effects during TEM characterization, which can substantially modify the structure and apparent morphology of ion tracks. Prolonged electron beam exposure promotes the recrystallization of initially amorphous tracks and surface hillocks, accompanied by the development of Fresnel contrast. These findings highlight the importance of understanding beam-induced transformations for the reliable interpretation of TEM observations of radiation-damaged materials.
relevance_reason: Combines TEM with molecular dynamics simulations of swift-heavy-ion tracks in rutile and anatase TiO2; explicit atoms (a), MD methodology (b), and application to track formation/recrystallization (c) are satisfied.

title: First-order correction to the self-consistent harmonic approximation free energy: Impact on the negative thermal expansion and phonon dynamics in ScF$_3$
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22538v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Strongly anharmonic crystals are often treated using the self-consistent harmonic approximation with variationally optimized Gaussian density matrices or the related self-consistent phonon theory. Both approaches capture substantial phonon renormalization but exclude connected non-Gaussian free-energy correlations. Here, we derive the first-order post-variational correction generated by the lowest non-vanishing normal-ordered residual vertex. Normal ordering the residual interaction around the optimized state shows that the linear and quadratic vertices vanish at the stationary variational solution, leaving a fluctuation-dressed cubic interaction whose second-order vacuum and two-point contractions generate the free-energy correction and the dynamical bubble self-energy, respectively. In ScF$_3$, the variational optimization on the full Born-Oppenheimer potential accounts for most of the shift in the thermal-expansion crossover temperature between negative and positive values relative to self-consistent phonon theory with a fourth-order potential. The connected correction changes the crossover modestly, but its volume derivative appreciably shifts the pressure-remapped cubic local-stability limit. Using the bare cubic vertex appears to improve agreement with the thermodynamic measurements, yet it systematically underestimates the measured zone-boundary tilt-mode energies at high temperatures. The fluctuation-dressed interaction gives more moderate thermodynamic corrections but yields phonon energies in better agreement with experiments. These results show that connected non-Gaussian correlations can significantly affect free-energy derivatives and soft-mode dynamics near a structural instability, and identify the optimized Gaussian state as the natural reference for constructing residual interactions beyond the stochastic self-consistent harmonic approximation.
relevance_reason: Derives a post-variational free-energy correction to the self-consistent harmonic approximation on the full Born-Oppenheimer (DFT) potential and applies it to anharmonic phonons and negative thermal expansion in ScF3; explicit atoms (a), DFT-based thermodynamics method development (b), and method advance with application (c) satisfied.

title: From a High-T$\rm_C$ Spin-Gapless Semiconductor to a Spin-Glass: The Role of Disorder in NiMnCrAl
abstract:
arXiv:2611.22784v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We combine first-principles calculations with structural, magnetic, and transport measurements to investigate the influence of chemical disorder on the quaternary Heusler alloy NiMnCrAl. For the ordered Y-type structure, density-functional-theory calculations predict a ferrimagnetic spin-gapless-semiconducting state with a total magnetic moment of $1.99\,\mu_{\mathrm{B}}/\mathrm{f.u.}$ and a mean-field ordering temperature of approximately $1300~\mathrm{K}$. Polycrystalline NiMnCrAl forms in a single average cubic phase; however, combined x-ray diffraction, neutron diffraction, and extended x-ray absorption fine-structure measurements reveal substantial antisite disorder, characterized by predominantly B2-like disorder with additional cross-sublattice mixing. No long-range ferrimagnetic transition is observed up to $700~\mathrm{K}$. Instead, the compound exhibits a broad magnetic anomaly near $37~\mathrm{K}$, frequency-dependent ac susceptibility, slow stretched-exponential relaxation, and field-cooled and zero-field-cooled memory effects, establishing a glassy magnetic state. The electrical resistivity is metallic and the Seebeck coefficient is negative, consistent with the loss of the ideal spin-gapless electronic structure. Exchange-interaction calculations show that antisite disorder introduces short Mn--Mn separations and competing antiferromagnetic Mn--Mn and Mn--Cr interactions, providing a microscopic basis for magnetic frustration. These results demonstrate the strong sensitivity to the predicted spin-gapless and ferrimagnetic states of NiMnCrAl to chemical disorder.
relevance_reason: Combines DFT first-principles calculations on explicit atomic structures with experiments to study disorder and magnetism in a Heusler alloy, satisfying (a)-(c) as an applied DFT materials study.

title: Systematic comparison of approximations and functionals in first-principle calculations of aluminum-based III-V ferroelectric nitrides
abstract:
arXiv:2605.24334v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We revisit first-principles predictions of structural, ferroelectric, and electronic properties in aluminum-based III-V nitride alloys, focusing on Al1-xScxN and Al1-xBxN. Using density functional theory within a unified 48-atom supercell framework, we systematically assess the role of chemical disorder and exchange-correlation approximations by comparing the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) and special quasirandom structures (SQS), as well as PBE, PBESol, SCAN, and SCAN+rVV10 functionals. We demonstrate that, even amongst the similar PBE and PBESol functionals, large quantitative and qualitative differences emerge. In particular, VCA or SQS PBESol modeling (a popular functional) underestimates the stability domain of the ferroelectric wurtzite phase in Al1-xScxN compared to SQS PBE or SQS SCAN. We demonstrate that the 5-fold coordinated hexagonal phase predicted in 2002 by Farrer and Bellaiche [Phys. Rev. B 66, 201203] is a metastable state whose energy lies between that of the four-fold coordinated ferroelectric wurtzite phase and the energy of the six-fold coordinated rocksalt phase below the transition point. In contrast, Al1-xBxN shows a much faster destabilization of the wurtzite ferroelectric phase, with bond breaking which strongly distorts the wurtzite structure (with enhanced polarization) and eventually favors a zincblende phase and a threefold coordinated hexagonal layer phase. Our analysis highlights the critical importance of both local disorder and exchange-correlation treatment in the quantitative prediction of the functional properties of III-V nitride ferroelectrics.
relevance_reason: DFT supercell calculations (PBE, PBESol, SCAN, SCAN+rVV10, VCA vs SQS) on explicit 48-atom AlScN/AlBN structures satisfy (a)-(c) and constitute a genuine functional/structural-model method comparison for ferroelectric nitride alloys.

title: Simulating catalytic resonance with molecular dynamics
abstract: Static heterogeneous catalysts are constrained by the Sabatier principle, where their overall turnover is limited by balancing the kinetics of reactant binding, surface reaction, and product unbinding. Modulating the surface binding energies between a strong binding state and a weak binding state can overcome this limit. For such a dynamic catalyst, a maximum turnover is achieved at a catalytic resonance modulating frequency. Here, we demonstrate that classical molecular simulation approaches can be used to study this phenomenon. Our method introduces a generic classical model for a surface reaction with time-dependent surface binding energy. Using a non-equilibrium molecular simulation in which reactants tend to be added to the system and products tend to be removed, we can simulate many catalyst cycles. Our approach reproduces catalytic resonance, with the dynamic catalyst providing up to a three-order-of-magnitude boost in turnover compared to the static catalyst. We further demonstrate the presence of a second resonant frequency in the gas phase, associated with resonance of the reacting bond. The general approach outlined here can be extended to more detailed models and used to study the molecular-scale effects of surface modulation and to computationally test input frequency, amplitude, and waveform for programmable catalysts.
relevance_reason: Classical non-equilibrium molecular simulation of a surface reaction with time-dependent binding energy satisfies (b) and likely (a) explicit particle/molecular representation, and applies it to catalytic resonance, satisfying (c).
